hints: Start by naming the functional group in each structure in every pair, ester, alcohol, ketone, alkane, alkene, carboxylic acid.
For pair A, ask which compound can be oxidised or can release hydrogen gas, the ester cannot react in either way.
For pair B, focus on the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group present in B1 but absent in the ester B2, and recall which test is specific for this group.
For pair C, recall the one classic test that distinguishes a saturated hydrocarbon from an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
For pair D, compare a neutral triol with a molecule containing $\text{COOH}$, and recall which base reacts only with acids to release a gas.
Remember you must use a different reagent for each of the four tests, so check you have four distinct reagents.
For each positive result, you must state both the visible observation such as colour change, precipitate or effervescence, and which compound gives it.
Check exact observations: orange to green for dichromate, yellow precipitate for iodoform, orange to colourless for bromine, effervescence for carbonate.
walkthrough:
Sort out pair A, ester versus secondary alcohol**
Look closely: A1 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, an ester, very unreactive to mild oxidation. A2 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, pentan-3-ol, a secondary alcohol. Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones by acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with colour change orange to green, or decolourise purple $\text{KMnO}_4$. With $\text{Na}$, the $\text{OH}$ gives effervescence of $\text{H}_2$. The ester does nothing, so the positive result identifies A2.

Sort out pair B, methyl ketone versus ester**
B1 is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, butan-2-one, which contains the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group. B2 is $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$, an ester with no such reactivity. Alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ gives a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ only with B1. Alternatively 2,4-DNPH gives a red, yellow or orange precipitate with the ketone B1 but no precipitate with the ester. So B1 is the positive compound.

Sort out pair C, alkane versus alkene**
C1 is cyclopentane, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$, saturated with only single bonds. C2 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, hex-2-ene, unsaturated. Aqueous bromine, $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$, is orange. Only the alkene undergoes electrophilic addition across the $\text{C=C}$ to give a colourless dibromoalkane, so C2 decolourises bromine. C1 shows no change.

Sort out pair D, triol versus hydroxy acid**
D1 is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$, only alcohol groups, neutral. D2 is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, contains a carboxylic acid group. $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{NaHCO}_3$ reacts only with acids: $2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. So D2 gives effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$, D1 gives no reaction.

Keep reagents distinct**
You have now used four different reagents: oxidising agent or sodium for A, alkaline iodine or 2,4-DNPH for B, bromine water for C, carbonate or hydrogencarbonate for D. That satisfies the instruction to use a different reagent for each test.

Final answer: Pair A: reagent $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ / $\text{KMnO}_4$ (acidified) OR $\text{Na}$; A2 positive: orange to green OR colourless OR effervescence.
Pair B: reagent alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ OR 2,4-DNPH; B1 positive: yellow precipitate OR red / yellow / orange precipitate.
Pair C: reagent $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$; C2 positive: turns orange to colourless.
Pair D: reagent $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ / $\text{NaHCO}_3$; D2 positive: effervescence.

hints: Decide whether cyclopentane, C1, has any permanent dipole or hydrogen bonding by looking at its C-H and C-C bonds only.
Link the strength of the only intermolecular force present to why little thermal energy is needed for melting and boiling.
walkthrough:
See why cyclopentane is nonpolar**
C1 is a pentagon ring of $\text{CH}_2$ groups. It has only $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds with very small electronegativity difference, no $\text{OH}$, no $\text{C=O}$, no permanent dipole and no hydrogen bonding. Think of it as a symmetrical hydrocarbon cloud.

Name the only force and link to low m.p. and b.p.**
The only attractions between molecules are London dispersion forces, also called instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, formed by momentary uneven electron distribution. These are very weak van der Waals forces. Melting and boiling only need to overcome these weak attractions, so little thermal energy is required. That is why melting point is $-94^{\circ}\text{C}$ and boiling point is only $+49^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: C1 is cyclopentane, a nonpolar hydrocarbon.
Only weak London / instantaneous dipole-induced dipole / dispersion forces exist between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them, giving low melting and boiling points.

hints: Recall that cis means the two H atoms on the $\text{C=C}$ are on the same side, with $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ also on the same side as each other.
walkthrough:
Draw cis-hex-2-ene correctly**
C2 is hex-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The double bond cannot rotate, so two geometries exist. For cis, put the $\text{C=C}$ horizontal, place both $\text{H}$ atoms both above the bond (or both below), and the two carbon chains $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ both on the opposite side together. That same-side arrangement is the cis isomer.
Final answer: cis-hex-2-ene: $\text{CH}_3\text{C(H)=C(H)(CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{CH}_3$ with both H atoms on the same side of the double bond (skeletal form showing cis geometry accepted).

hints: Ask whether C2, an alkene, joins by opening its double bond with no small molecule lost, or by condensation with loss of water.
walkthrough:
Recognise addition from the C=C**
C2 has one $\text{C=C}$ double bond and no other functional groups that could lose water. When heated gently the pi bond opens and monomers join directly with no by-product. That is the definition of addition polymerisation.

hints: Remember to change the double bond in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to a single bond and add extension bonds on both carbons.
Check that $\text{CH}_3$ and H are on the first carbon and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and H are on the second carbon of the repeat unit.
walkthrough:
Build the backbone from the monomer**
Take $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH(CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{CH}_3$ and open the double bond to a single bond. Each doubly bonded carbon now forms two single bonds along the chain. Draw $\text{-C-C-}$ with a dangling bond at each end to show continuation: $\text{-CH-CH-}$.

Attach the side groups correctly**
The left carbon originally carried $\text{CH}_3$ and H, so the repeat unit has $\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-}$. The right carbon originally carried $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and H, so it becomes $\text{-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)-}$. Put together: $\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)-}$. No double bond remains.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)-}$ shown with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons, with $\text{CH}_3$ and H on one carbon and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and H on the other.
